payload.text: Genesis AI , a startup teaching robots to perform physical tasks by learning from human movements, announced Tuesday it has raised $500 million in Series A funding at a $3.5 billion valuation. Premji Invest , Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the round, which brings the company’s disclosed funding to $605 million since its 2024 inception. Genesis previously raised $105 million in a round announced in July 2025. The company is developing both robots and the AI software that controls them. Its approach combines recordings of human hand movements with training in simulated environments, where robots can practice skills before attempting them in the physical world. Genesis is initially targeting manufacturing, logistics and laboratories with its robot, Eno. Zhou Xian and Theophile Gervet, co-founders of Genesis AI. (Courtesy photo) “We just want to bring something more elegant, more timeless,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian told Crunchbase News in an interview. “In the end, this is a very full-stack company. … We have to build all different pieces across the entire stack to make sure we can tightly integrate our technology stack together, and hopefully build the most well-polished and reliable product. Other participants in the new financing include T. Rowe Price Associates , Durable Capital Partners , Bpifrance , HSG , Nvidia , AMD Ventures , Zoom , Samsung Next and Ericsson . Individual backers include Eric Schmidt , Eric Yuan , Jerry Yang , Xavier Niel and Zach Kirkhorn . The company plans to use the capital to expand its computing infrastructure, increase robot production and hire more employees, Xian told Crunchbase News. Presently, Genesis has close to 100 employees. It is headquartered in Paris, with offices in San Carlos, California. Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with most of the investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data. The closely related field of physical AI has also seen a surge in venture investment this year. Learning from human movements Genesis’s approach grew out of a challenge Xian encountered during his robotics research: The difficulty of finding enough examples for robots to learn from. Language models have vast amounts of text to draw on. But robots need a different kind of data to learn how to move and for example, pick up and handle objects. They also need that data to better understand what they’re touching and what happens when they act. Genesis works by using cameras and gloves to capture people’s hand and finger movements as they work, along with touch information. The company says its robotic hand closely matches the human hand and recording glove, making it easier for robots to learn those movements. Historically, collecting this kind of training data involves hiring people to remotely control robots, Xian said. Genesis aims to collect it from people doing their regular jobs instead. Those recordings help train the company’s AI model, GENE. Genesis also uses its simulation software, Genesis World, to train and test robot skills in virtual environments. The company claims this speeds up a process that would take longer with physical machines alone. From research project to robotics startup Genesis traces its origins to a research collaboration Xian started in 2022, also named Genesis, while he was pursuing a robotics Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University . The project brought together researchers from more than a dozen universities to develop robotics simulation tools. After graduating at the end of 2024, Xian teamed up with Theophile Gervet and decided to start a company. Genesis formally launched in March 2025 and expanded beyond simulation into AI software and robot hardware. Xian said developing those components together would help Genesis make them work reliably as a finished product. “That requires the intelligence, hardware and everything that goes into training and testing the robots to work as one system,” he said. Renting robots to businesses Genesis is exploring a rental model in which customers would pay for the robot and its software as a combined service. It has announced a partnership with LG CNS and has other Fortune 500 companies in its prospective customer pipeline, according to Xian. He declined to disclose revenue and did not provide a paying customer count. Premji Invest partner Vedant Agrawal said in a release that the firm was drawn to demonstrations of robots completing extended tasks independently. “Completing full tasks in real time, not just short clips, is what turns a robot into something a business can rely on,” he said. Genesis says it is ramping up Eno production for industrial customers. Looking ahead, it plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare, then consumer and outdoor uses. payload.text: By Kelly Meerbott The round closes. The announcement goes out. For about a week, everyone is happy. Then the pressure doubles. The number that used to be a hope is now a promise. The board that used to be patient now has a timeline. And the founder who just finished the hardest sales job of their life is expected to make the best decisions of their life, immediately, on less sleep than they’ve had in months. I’ve spent 17 years coaching about 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders. The pattern repeats often enough that I treat the first 90 days after a raise as a danger window. Founders don’t get complacent in that window. They get flooded, and most of them won’t say so out loud. What pressure does to judgment Kelly Meerbott of YOU – Loud & Clear. Neuroscientist Amy Arnsten’s review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience puts it plainly: “even quite mild acute uncontrollable stress can cause a rapid and dramatic loss of prefrontal cognitive abilities.” The prefrontal cortex weighs options and holds a plan steady. Notice the word uncontrollable. After a raise, a founder controls less than the cap table suggests: the hiring market, customer timelines, the board’s expectations. The founder hasn’t become less intelligent. The judgment that built the company is just harder to reach. Porcelli and Delgado , writing in Psychological Science, stressed volunteers with a hand in ice water then offered them financial gambles. They grew more cautious about potential gains and more willing to gamble on potential losses. It was a lab study, but I see the same shape in a founder six weeks after a Series B: hesitant about the bets that justified the round, and suddenly willing to roll the dice on anything that feels like a threat. The decisions that go wrong in this window rarely feel reckless. They feel rational, because the nervous system is treating uncertainty like an emergency. Where it shows up Senior hiring. An investor who advises 20 fast-growing technology startups told me one of the biggest sources of leadership friction he sees is a CEO hiring a head of sales because they know the person. The relationship feels safe, so the offer is generous. Then the results don’t come. Under pressure, familiarity feels like certainty. But knowing someone isn’t the same as knowing they can lead sales at the company’s next stage. Expansion. Pressure condenses time. The new market planned for month 12 moves to month three. The data didn’t change. Waiting became unbearable. One founder I coached pulled a 12-month expansion into three, bragged about how little sleep he was getting, and did everything himself. The second-market launch was a sloppy, drama-filled disaster. The board brought me in to put him back together and triage the launch. Ask whether the evidence changed or your tolerance for uncertainty did. Co-founder relationships. Harvard Business School professor Noam Wasserman, who studied 10,000 founders for “The Founder’s Dilemmas,” has put the share of high-potential startups that fail because of co-founder conflict at 65%. One founder withdraws because they’re overwhelmed. The other interprets the silence as distrust. A trauma-informed lens doesn’t treat every disagreement as trauma. It builds enough trust that a disagreement doesn’t become one more emergency. Four habits that protect judgment Make the decision window a rule, not a mood. For the first 90 days, don’t finalize a senior hire, a market entry or an equity change in the meeting where you first propose it. Write down the criteria, then sleep on it. Name the state before the decision. Before a major call, ask: Where am I on a pressure scale of 1 to 10? Not how the business is doing. How much you’re carrying. A high number earns the decision a second conversation. Put the avoided conversation on the calendar. Co-founders get 30 minutes a week on how each of them is doing, not just what they’re doing. Laptops closed. Give the board a better question. Ask the founder: “What decision are you about to make that you wouldn’t make rested?” Then help slow that one down. The founder to watch If you sit on the board, the week the wire clears is when you start paying attention. Composure can mean steadiness. It can also hide exhaustion. The founders who come through this window well tend to have one person outside the cap table, the org chart and the family they can think out loud with before a decision hardens. Investor Matt Cohen has written here that founders often have no one inside their company to confide in. Founders, who is that person for you right now? If you can’t name one, that’s useful information too. The capital is in the account. The open question is whether the person deciding how to spend it can still reach the judgment that raised it. Find that out before the first big decision, not after. Executive coach Kelly Meerbott is principal of YOU – Loud & Clear . Her performance coaching is trauma-informed, neuroscience-backed and somatic. For more than 17 years she has coached roughly 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders, Fortune 500 executives, and more than 500 senior military leaders. She was named Top Coach in America in 2025, is a TEDx speaker, and has written for Fast Company , Training Magazine and Hotel Executive. She is based in Narberth, Pennsylvania, and holds Professional Certified Coach and Certified Clinical Trauma Specialist certifications. title: PwC’s IPO Lead On A Selective Market, AI Valuations And The Outlook For 2027

Companies seeking to go public face investors focused on durable revenue, profitability and valuation, while uncertainty has prompted some issuers to postpone their offerings. payload.text: The U.S. IPO market has rebounded, but the recovery remains uneven. Companies seeking to go public face investors focused on durable revenue, profitability and valuation, while uncertainty has prompted some issuers to postpone their offerings. Mike Bellin , a partner and U.S. IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers , sees a market that remains open to companies with the right scale, financial metrics and preparation. In a recent conversation with Crunchbase News, Bellin discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest. He also outlined what could set the stage for a stronger start to 2027. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Crunchbase News: How healthy is the IPO market right now? Mike Bellin, US IPO services leader, PricewaterhouseCooper. (Courtesy photo) Bellin: A good IPO year in the U.S. is anywhere from 125 to 175 traditional IPOs, and year to date we’ve seen just south of 90 or so. The breadth of the market shows me that it’s been a healthy market. We’ve seen industrial products come back to market. We’ve seen tech, consumer markets, energy, utilities and some financial services come back to market. For the majority of the first three quarters of the year, it was a pretty strong and broad IPO market. But the momentum has halted significantly since September and October. Is the market in trouble? I would say no. It’s very selective. It’s not shut. Quality issuers with readiness, the right story, the right metrics can still get their deals done. What has contributed to the slowdown? Bellin: The macro environment in general was the big mover: rates, inflation, geopolitical concerns. Just that uncertainty was a big factor. One of the big factors that I’ve seen is valuation. Some fairly aggressive valuations were being asked for in certain transactions, certain offerings, and I think the market — with all those uncertainties that I mentioned — was looking at those valuations and thinking it was maybe a bit rich. I believe many issuers decided to hit pause and wait for another window to open. What are public market investors looking for? Bellin: What investors are really looking for is durable revenue — revenue that’s backed up by strong customers, diverse customers and a growing revenue base. I think it’s that revenue reliability where there is a significant backlog of demand for the product, the services of the IPO issuer. That’s always a strong sign. The other item is leverage. For companies with significant leverage in a rising-rate environment, the questions are: Can they take on new leverage that creates profitable value opportunities going forward? Can they refinance existing leverage given rates are higher? Making sure that you’re going into the capital markets with a reasonable leverage ratio, or explaining through your equity story how you’re getting a return on the capital that you have invested from a debt perspective, makes a significant difference. Is the market open to a broad range of venture-backed startups, or primarily larger companies? Bellin: Scale matters. Companies that have that scale, whether it’s from a revenue perspective or an asset-based perspective, depending on the sector, make a big difference. Those are the types of companies that can almost dictate the window that they’re going to go out in and do well. Some of the smaller companies, the midmarket companies, smaller-cap companies — again, outside of life science and biotechs — they’ve been a little bit challenged. If you’re growing at the right rate, you’re showing the right metrics, the IPO market is fully available to those types of companies. But if you’re still on the lower-scale side of the house, your opportunities may be limited to hit the market. Will enthusiasm for AI companies carry into public markets, or will investors be more skeptical? Bellin: I think investors aren’t skeptical of AI; they’re skeptical of spend without visibility — visibility to future earnings, visibility to that revenue durability that I mentioned. The market is separating AI companies with visible demand from the ones with only a narrative out there, and I think that demand, that growth, the backlog is key. The other factor we’re seeing in today’s market again comes down to cash generation and profitability. If you’re not profitable, when will that profitable period come? Profitability comes in many different measures. Could be GAAP income, could be EBITDA income, but also cash flows and free cash flows and levered free cash flows that are available to the company. We haven’t seen a period like this of development, of growth, ever before. It’s exciting, but I do think the market will discern between those companies that are public-company worthy and those that are not. What does the uneven performance of newly public companies signal? Bellin: It signals selectivity. There have been some really big winners in the IPO market, and others that, post-issuance, haven’t traded as well as many expected. Many of the companies that are coming to market have to be very thoughtful on the valuation and what you’re going to go price at. If you’re trying to be too aggressive on pricing, you may trade down post-IPO, which is going to impact those metrics. Overall, we’re seeing strong candidates come to market. I do think companies are coming to market better prepared now than ever, given this volatility. What is driving biotech’s resurgence? Bellin: The M&A market for many of these companies is very strong today. As some of the larger health company names lose the patents to some of the profitable drugs, they’re looking at that next generation of development and where there could be value. Many of these biotechs were purchased by large pharma companies even before coming to the public markets. That competition for these assets and companies is creating a nice horse trade between an IPO opportunity with a lot of upside and an M&A exit with more certainty day one. I think M&A is the engine behind the IPO market’s resurgence for these companies. In the IPO markets, many of these assets have traded very well, and that’s where the momentum and that flywheel effect in the IPO market is very important. We’ve seen that flywheel and that momentum in biotech. We haven’t seen it in the rest of the market in the last couple of months. Why are SPACs attracting renewed interest? Bellin: With market volatility, we’re seeing more conversations around SPACs. Because SPACs set valuation certainty on day one, a company looking to exit via SPAC understands the potential cash that may come their way. It’s not certain, of course, given redemptions, etc. Another factor driving a healthy SPAC market may be these serial SPAC issuers. They understand the SPAC product. They understand what makes a good de-SPAC candidate, and they know whether the target company can be ready, show growth and hit the milestones that may be discussed in the offering document. The market is healthier and more mature today than in the past. That said, we’re still seeing many SPACs continue to look for a target, given the massive SPAC inventory available to target companies. What do you expect in 2027? Bellin: Hundreds of companies are in the pipeline, and they’re ready to go when the market is. Much of the remainder of ’26, and the start of 2027, depends on market momentum. I’m an eternal optimist. There’s a lot of demand on the buy side; there’s still significant capital available to the right companies. So if we can create that momentum here in the remaining months of 2026, I think we’re going to see a strong start to 2027. The AI ecosystem that we’ve been talking about is healthy. Demand for energy is always significant, and the right energy companies are coming to market. Consumer and industrial products — those are coming back. Private equity has been very active in ’26, and I’d expect them to continue that activity in 2027. I think we’re in for a strong year, but it will remain selective. payload.text: A few months ago, I was sitting lakeside with a neighbor. He is the head of AI for a pharmaceutical company, and he mentioned the truly incredible productivity his senior team is receiving from AI. Then he paused and turned to me and said: “You know, I may never hire another junior engineer again. Which is great for the business right now, but who’s the next generation that is going to run this when we retire?” The concern over what will happen to young people just entering the workforce is one many of us are grappling with right now, and it has a human dimension. Not just what happens to employment rates, but what happens to my students or my children? College graduates typically do the individual contributor knowledge work that AI is evermore capable of delivering. To cite one statistic , a recent Stanford study found employment of 22 to 25 year olds in occupations most exposed to AI is running 19% below rates for their peers in less AI-impacted sectors, and that gap has been widening. What role will new graduates play in the age of AI? And how will we develop the generation of managers who will supervise AI? Fortunately, we have thriving examples with 200 years of history on how to teach 22 year olds to do exactly that. Our claim is that the reason senior folks get more out of AI today is not primarily because they have greater subject knowledge, but rather because they are good managers. They have to trust folks who work for them without completely trusting them, they have to divide tasks, delegate clearly, check results and patiently correct, coach, and sometimes shift personnel on their teams. The future for new graduates is to become great managers now, at the very beginning of their career, and not after a long period of individual contribution. The craft of management The nature of the innovation of AI is that it delivers knowledge work. We know a lot about human knowledge workers and the analogy to AI knowledge workers is strong. Knowledge workers know much more about their individual sphere of expertise than their managers do. Good managers routinely organize and lead knowledge workers who are just flat-out much smarter than they are. They do this through the craft of management. These same qualities, as AI behaves more like AI executives , naturally give good managers the skills to manage AI agents, who become the individual contributor knowledge workers. It is no secret that the investment industry culture values most highly the brilliance of the individual contributor who delivers the incisive observation, makes the correct investment call, and closes the one-on-one negotiation with a win. I have lived this culture for a long time. Calling an investor a “great people manager” is a backhanded compliment at best. In the investment industry, the jump from individual contributor to manager usually arrives midcareer or later, and typically with little to no formal training in the craft of management. The analyst, associate and vice president are primarily acting as individual contributors (though of course they may mentor a few junior folks), and are not shifting to acting primarily as managers of other knowledge workers until principal or perhaps partner. When I was an analyst at Morgan Stanley many years ago, the hierarchy ran from analyst to managing director. Analysts were the ultimate individual contributors, and whenever an analyst would attempt to delegate some work to others, we had a name for that: “managing analyst.” This clever put-down reflected the cultural belief that real credit goes to those who do, not those who deliver through the work of those they manage. What happens without management This blind spot on the importance of management is not limited to the investment industry. As another salient recent example, let’s look at the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident . Much has been written about this event, where OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face . In OpenAI’s own report on the incident, its proposed long list of fixes, including stronger security, alerts on breaches and post-incident remediation, does not address directly training its employees to be better managers of these agents. That’s even as the company acknowledges that members of an internal team at OpenAI knew of many of the concerning behaviors (including message board and unauthorized internet access) in late May, and did not act until July. This may be an unfair analogy, but imagine if we hired 1,200 workers to operate a warehouse complex, gave each of them detailed written instructions, and then had all the line managers and senior managers leave for a week. If we came back to find that someone had stolen a delivery van, the problem wouldn’t be that these weren’t the right workers or that the instructions weren’t clear enough. The problem is lack of management. Accelerated leadership development Michael Quoia, co-founder and partner at KSE Leadership. As I was wrestling with this problem, I talked with my business school classmate Michael Quoia, who attended the U.S. Naval Academy and served as an officer, and then built a career in executive leadership development. He recalled: “When I met my division of 25 sailors in Yokosuka, Japan at the young age of 22 years old, I was greeted by my senior chief petty officer, who already served for nearly 20 years. Behind him, we had several organizational levels including the first line sailors who conducted maintenance on the fire control systems. This was actually a harder problem than we are facing with AI. This was about supervising at least three levels without experience. I was expected to provide character, judgment, problem solving and leadership, despite not having come up through the ranks. How did the Navy develop these qualities in me so that I could bypass time in the seat as a frontline worker?” Like companies facing the AI dilemma we have been exploring, the military needs to develop capable leaders who lack entry-level experience. And while the military is a very relevant example, it is not the only one. The Home Depot ’s store management program and General Electric ’s Crotonville are two examples of corporations who recruit high-potential talent and put them through an accelerated leadership development program to prepare them to lead people in jobs they have not done. Let’s look, though, at how the Naval Academy provided Michael’s training, and what that may mean whether you are 22 years old or hiring 22-year-olds. First, the foundation of developing future officers is the development of moral leadership. The mission of the United States Naval Academy begins with the phrase “To develop midshipmen morally, mentally, and physically … .” In an age of AI, first-line managers of AI agents will need integrity and a moral compass, because AI does not come with that reliably pre-installed. It is no overstatement to suggest that moral leadership of AI could have societal implications and needs to be developed. Second, the service academies are intentionally designed as leadership laboratories. From plebe summer to commissioning, midshipmen progress from learning how to be a good subordinate to true manager. What is most relevant to the age of AI is that simulated leadership learning is possible and proven if designed with care. Third, the service academies build high-pressure situations into their leadership laboratory. While most companies are not placing their first-line managers in life or death situations, the ability to lead in high stakes situations, for instance to take personal responsibility for an AI agent swarm you launched which is now “going rogue,” requires composure and decisiveness under stress and pressure. Bring back the ‘managing analyst’ If a 22-year-old ensign can manage 25 sailors on a Yokosuka destroyer, albeit with support from senior officers and enlisted, our 22-year-old college graduate can certainly be trained to manage 25 super-intelligent agents. The moment for practicing the craft of management will shift from 32 years old to 22 years old, across the businesses of knowledge work. In short: We need to bring back the “managing analyst.” We need to recognize that AI agents behave like knowledge workers and therefore need to be managed. We should reset the culture in knowledge work industries that management is a valued skill, beginning at the start of one’s career and not midcareer. These entry-level workers are smart, motivated, learn quickly and work hard. There is a huge unmet need for the craft of management in corralling this new generation of AI agents. We have the proof points across nearly 200 years from our service academies that these skills can be taught to the young, and the young can deliver them with distinction. The future for college graduates is a redefinition of their jobs away from being individual-contributor knowledge workers and toward being effective managers and leaders from the very beginning of their careers. Bob Morse co-founded Strattam Capital in 2014 and is managing partner. He has served on numerous private and public technology company boards, and currently is a director of CloudHesive , Contegix , Daxtra Technologies , Green Security , Resource Navigation and Trax Group . Previously, he was a partner and member of the investment committee at Oak Hill Capital Partners . He also worked at GCC Investments and Morgan Stanley . In robotics and manufacturing, Plural has backed Monumental , which develops bricklaying robots; Sunrise Robotics , which builds robots for manufacturing; CircuitHub , which manufactures circuit board assemblies; and Upside Robotics , which develops agricultural robots. In compute, its investments include optical AI accelerator company Olix and photonic networking company Oriole Networks . More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum , which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute. Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, said Tamkivi. “Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the big labs are in the U.S. and China,’  and so forth. payload.text: Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026. The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data , already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor. With co-founder Jensen Huang ’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China , we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold. A widening investment footprint Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall. Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year , when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior. The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI ’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic ’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.) The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI . Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion. Beyond the biggest AI labs NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers. The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI ’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi ’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics , which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc . As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data. For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers. The question of what comes next Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership. payload.text: In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition. In reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat. Fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week , both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat. The looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test. The verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception. Our findings below: No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert : Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor. That said, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food. Made by: Medici Brands ( David parent company). No. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda : The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can. But what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d plan to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein. Made by: SkyPop (formerly Don’t Quit) No. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn : Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving. Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose. Made by: Khloud No. 4 Mosh : In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he launched with his mother, Maria Shriver . The Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not. I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you might eat if you wanted that particular nutrient mix. But it’s not something to consume for pleasure. Made by: Mosh No. 5 Cadootz Crackers : We tried two varieties of Cadootz Crackers — cheddar and sea salt — and walked away neither enthused nor repulsed. For people interested in a gluten- and seed oil-free small snack cracker with about 5 grams of protein per serving, Cadootz rises to the occasion. It’s got a nice crunch and decent flavor. As someone who’s not particularly seeking to avoid gluten and seed oils or to get a modest protein bump from my crackers, I’ll probably pass on follow-on purchases. But for its target audience, Cadootz should serve well. Made by: Cadootz! No. 6 Frozen One : For those who thought the David frozen dessert was a marvel of protein engineering, the folks at Frozen One would like a word. Their protein ice cream has a whopping 40 grams of protein in each pint. Yes, but how does it taste? Not that bad, according to our two-person tasting team. We tried both the chocolate and apple pie varieties, preferring the former. Like the David offering, Frozen One tastes like a product made with milk protein concentrate and sugar substitutes. You won’t mistake it for Ben and Jerry’s . But if the goal is to consume a steak-like quantity of protein in the form factor of a pint of ice cream, it does its job. Made by: Frozen One No. 7 Brami Protein Pasta : We saved the best for last. That, unexpectedly, was Brami Protein Pasta, a noodle made from semolina and lupini beans that boasts about 70% more protein than standard pasta and more than double the fiber. With about 12 grams of protein for a 200 calorie serving, Brami isn’t a dense protein source. But, with the right topping, it’s enough to transform a typically starchy noodle meal into something reasonably protein rich. Most notably, however, Brami tastes quite good, with no discernable weird aftertaste or texture issues. I made both standard and Brami noodles to taste the difference. For seconds, I went with the Brami. Made by: Brami Related Crunchbase query: Protein Snacks And Packaged Foods Startups Related reading: VCs Are Still Chasing Protein, Even As Fake Meat Falls Out Of Favor Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: By Yakov Filippenko One day, I woke up to a notice that our app had been removed from Apple’s App Store. For the next month or so, we racked our brains trying to find out why. We even reached out to our internal contacts, only for them to tell us that helping us could put their jobs at risk. Nothing seemed to work. For years, the App Store’s unwritten contract seemed simple. As long as you followed the guidelines, your storefront would remain available. Then a removal notice arrives, and you wonder whether your business can survive. In 2025, Apple removed 166,899 apps and reported just 423 restorations after appeals. As we learned, being caught in it feels like watching your business collapse, with no guarantee of recovery. It’s not all bad news, though. We survived, and this episode taught me that platform dependency is ultimately infrastructure risk. As founders, we prepare for cloud outages and payment failures, but losing access to the platform that brings us customers deserves the same attention. Fortunately, we were prepared, and this is how you can be, too. Understand what a removal can take away Yakov Filippenko, founder and CEO at Intch. First, prospective customers can no longer download your app. Then, paying subscribers flood support with a more damaging question. “The app is gone. Are you a scam?” The bloodshed continues as existing users replace their phones and can’t reinstall the app, eroding your customer base. Financially, Apple immediately freezes funds from the previous three months and turns off recurring subscriptions. For a subscription-dependent company, this can send its monthly recurring revenue to zero. Before spending another cent on acquisition, consider what would happen to those customers if your app disappeared tomorrow. Could they still use your product and continue paying you? If the answer is no, every new customer makes your business more dependent on a platform decision you cannot control. Don’t make an appeal your contingency plan Cal AI , reportedly generating $100,000 daily, was pulled without warning and later reappeared. But its reinstatement tells you little about how long your business might wait. In Intch ’s case, the explanation was so generic it told us nothing. We had 30 days to appeal, but the process ended with a canned rejection. Your appeal may succeed, but your business must operate while you wait. Preparing in advance lets you keep going, whatever the outcome. Build the alternative before you need it Our experience was grueling, but fortunately, two years earlier we had decoupled from the App Store by building a web version and making it our primary payment channel. It also let us ship updates 10 times a day while escaping Apple’s predatory commissions. We weren’t the only ones. Pavel Durov , founder of Telegram , has also promoted web access to bypass store restrictions and potential censorship. The lesson is straightforward. Customers need a working alternative before access disappears. Building one only after removal leaves the business exposed while the team races to replace its storefront. We initially feared the user experience would suffer, but that concern proved unfounded. After the removal, every key metric fully recovered. If you share this concern, test it while your app is still available to see whether customers can use and pay for the web version before they must rely on it. Include platform exposure in growth decisions Most founders see the App Store as a distribution channel, but rarely account for how much control it gives Apple over their business. Before investing more in growth, examine how much revenue depends on continued access and what would survive a removal. Know how long the company could survive an unanswered appeal. Investors should ask those questions too, because a growing subscription base deserves closer scrutiny when a single platform decision can interrupt its revenue. That exposure belongs in funding and valuation discussions. Monopolies act in their interests, and if your business falls outside their vision, you may have little say in a decision that could destroy it. You cannot control it, but you can decide whether it has the power to end your company. By building an alternative while your app is still available, you’ve made the wisest choice. Yakov Filippenko is a seasoned entrepreneur with more than 10 years of experience in IT and technologies, as well as scaling businesses internationally. As a product manager at Yandex , he led a team that grew the product’s user base from 500,000 to 1.2 million and secured its entry into the international market. Subsequently, he co-founded SailPlay , which he scaled to 45 countries and eventually exited, after it was acquired by Retail Rocket in 2018. In 2021, Filippenko launched Intch , an AI-powered platform connecting part-time professionals with flexible roles. Illustration: Dom Guzman

For everything from sodas to snack bars to pasta, it’s now standard practice for food and drink makers to play up protein content whenever feasible. While we may cut carbs and fret over fat, most of us are still keen on protein. Startups and their backers have been riding this trend too. Over the past decade, investors have poured billions into upstarts promising cheaper, tastier and more sustainable ways to meet our protein quotas. Unfortunately, many of their earlier bets have fared poorly. Vast sums poured into lab-grown meat several years ago, for instance, have so far failed to produce a success story. Former high-flying plant-based meat startups Beyond (now public) and Impossible Foods have seen their valuations wither. Others have shuttered. In response, more recent startup investment has shifted away from meat substitutes and toward stuffing more protein into other packaged foods and drinks. It’s a fad that’s obvious on supermarket shelves, where startups and established brands alike relentlessly tout the added protein in their noodles, pancakes, cereals, energy bars, popcorn and so on. Deal flow looks robust In startup circles, protein-related investment looks tiny in comparison to the billions bet on AI. Deal flow, however, remains fairly robust, with Crunchbase identifying a few dozen protein-focused startups funded in the past year. Moreover, some of these rounds are quite sizable, like a $250 million September Series B for Medici Brands , maker of David Protein snack bars. To illustrate, we used Crunchbase data to put together sample sets of recently-funded protein-focused companies across several themes. These include packaged foods, drinks, ingredients and processes, and animal feed. Protein snacks and packaged foods Snacks and packaged foods look like the largest fundraisers among protein startups, securing hundreds of millions in the past year. For a sense of who’s raising, we put together a list of seven recently funded brands that are finding their way to store shelves. The bulk of recent funding went to the aforementioned parent of David Protein. That brand, in addition to churning sweet-flavored bars with a protein content to rival cod , has been expanding into ice cream and milkshakes. Wilde Brands , which makes crackers from chicken breasts, has also proven popular with investors, pulling in $40 million last month. Among early-stage startups, meanwhile, Frozen One has been off to a brisk start, raising over $8 million for a line of high-protein ice creams now selling at Target . Protein drinks Startups and investors are also catering to people who want their high-protein diet in drinkable form. To illustrate, we put together six recently funded examples below. Ripple Foods , which makes a vegan milk using pea protein, is the highest historical funding recipient, raising over $300 million in its 12-year-history, even though it hasn’t officially joined the unicorn club. Clear protein drinks are also increasingly a thing, with multiple startups including protein soda brand Juuz and sports drink purveyor Protein2o . Precision fermentation and plant protein ingredients Quite a few funded startups are focused more on novel, protein-rich ingredients rather than their own branded retail lineup. In many cases, they’re using precision fermentation to deliver. We put together seven examples below. The Every Co. , which makes animal-free egg white proteins through fermentation, is the biggest funding recipient and one of the older names on our list. It’s raised nearly $300 million in the past 10 years, including a $55 million round a year ago. Early stage is also seeing some action from startups including Edonia , which makes a high-protein cooking ingredient from spirulina, Animal feed and pet food A number of funded protein startups are also focusing on pets and livestock — a target audience that’s not quite so overwhelmed by supermarket options. To illustrate, we aggregated five such companies that raised funding in recent quarters. Notably, two of them — InnovaFeed and nextProtein — are bug-focused. InnovaFeed has raised over $500 million to raise insects for feeding livestock, pet food and aquaculture. NextProtein is using fly larvae for feedstock. Others are focused on pets. Meatly , for instance, secured a Series A round this spring to build what it says will be Europe’s largest cultivated meat facility. It plans to partner with pet food brands and sell its own branded lineup once production scales. Broad focus: Protein, not meat If we were to encapsulate a broad trend across most of the protein-related financings it would be that startups aren’t trying to convince people that vegetables are meat. Rather, they’re focused largely on protein as an in-demand macronutrient that can be increasingly concentrated and stuffed into a bewildering variety of flavors and form factors. That might not all taste as good as their more sugary, high-fat and carb-laden alternatives, but at least they’ve got protein. title: TrnRT
summary: An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium

extra.author: sanchitmonga22
extra.original_title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium

story_text.value:
Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :)

What it does today:

- Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router.

- Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks.

- Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance.

We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results.

But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now.

We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions:

- 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency)

-The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps.

Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels.

So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8.

The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within

There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections.

You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results:

https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega...

Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback.

Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai.

We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

title: tamserve
summary: Open-source, real-time object tracking for live video feeds

extra.author: aryaman_darda
extra.original_title: Show HN: Open-source, real-time object tracking for live video feeds

story_text.value:
I type "forklift" on a live warehouse camera, and tamserve finds and tracks both forklifts, including the one driving in. Then I add "person" without stopping it.

tamserve runs Meta's SAM 3 on live camera feeds. SAM 3's own tracker handles one recorded video at a time, runs at about 8 fps, and runs out of memory on long videos. tamserve uses SAM 3 to find objects every few frames and a lightweight tracker (EdgeTAM) to follow them in between, with one copy of each model shared across all your cameras.

*On one RTX 4090:*

* *Any object you name:* 4x faster than SAM 3's tracker, at 92% of its accuracy * *People:* 16 cameras at once, 14x less GPU per frame, and slightly more accurate than SAM 3 (89.6 vs 87.8 HOTA) * *Memory:* flat at 3.5 GB on a 3,000 frame video, where SAM 3 runs out at frame 423

*Worth a look if you're building:*

* Warehouse or factory safety (forklifts, pallets, hard hats) * Security or retail camera analytics * Home or elder care monitoring * Robotics, wildlife or lab monitoring * Annotation tools for long videos

`pip install "tamserve[sam3]"`

Please give me any and all feedback or edit tamserve to meet your needs, and a star helps if you find it useful!

title: Goethe
summary: turn your computer into an inference engine

extra.author: matteohorvath
extra.original_title: Show HN: Goethe – turn your computer into an inference engine

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Matteo from meshapplied (YC W27), building this with Peter and Janos.

We think you can and should own your inference, so we built software that actually supports that. Goethe turns a Linux machine with an NVIDIA GPU into an API your OpenAI, Anthropic compatible clients can call.

``` curl -fsSL https://goethe.sh/install.sh | bash goethe start ```

Limits: it's Linux only rn and it supports Ampere or newer NVIDIA GPUs. Logging in with `goethe login` is optional and turns on the optimized kernels.

Docs: [goethe.sh/docs](https://goethe.sh/docs)

I'd love to hear what breaks and what you'd want next.

title: box
summary: One cloud computer for all your agents

extra.author: taro666
extra.original_title: Show HN: One cloud computer for all your agents

story_text.value:
Hi HN, my team just released box by Simular, a cloud computer for all your agents, with fast computer use built-in.

box gives your agents one remote Ubuntu desktop with Chrome and a shell, which your AI can then drive over MCP while your own computer stays unoccupied.

That means you can turn your basic ChatGPT plan into a personal agent by giving it a box computer; let your Claude Code pick up what Codex has left off on the same box to maximize usage; actually close your laptop and let tasks run in one persistent, 24/7 environment with all your logins and setup.

Some box demos: https://x.com/SimularAI/status/2121329778896871665?a=U4U1yYT...

We started on this because we believe computers shouldn't need human operation in the future. When agents arrived, people started running them on mini computers and you see colleagues walk around the office with their laptop lid open. We think there's a better solution - cloud computers engineered for agents.

Simular started three years ago to build out the full stack of an autonomous computer. box is our attempt to give agents a body to live in.

Our computer use outperformed Opus and GPT on OSWorld, costing fewer tokens. https://thenewstack.io/sai-agent-osworld-benchmark/

Copy/paste one command into your agent to start:

"Set up box from https://box.simular.ai/install"

You can watch box's live action from a dashboard https://box.simular.ai/box

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. I'll be in comments here to answer any question.

title: Fakemetrics.com
summary: "build in public" like a superstar

extra.author: tigranbs
extra.original_title: Show HN: Fakemetrics.com – "build in public" like a superstar

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I am Tigran (github.com/tigranbs)
I made Fakemetrics.com as a fun experiment while testing how well Claude Opus can build pixel-identical UIs. It turned out it wasn't as easy as just prompting it, but I spent time building the system so it works almost every time.
And I am pretty sure you are seeing a bunch of people posting weekend vibe-coded apps and saying "$50K/month after quitting my McDonnalds job...". Well, even my friend tried to fake it a few months back.
So, I kinda did this fakemetrics.com as an experiment to see how well I can have the system that clones UIs, and packaged that as a very simple (I think) usable product for the people that want to be a superstar "build in public" type of a person with no revenue, but a perfect Stripe user growth screenshot.
Useful? - Probably not that much
Fun? - YES!!
The best part is that Claude, ChatGPT, or Grok models aren't that good at UI clones by default, but with fakemetrics.com I kinda made a system that produces near-identical results from screenshots fairly fast. That was worth learning!
Let me know what you think? Should I move on with the UI cloning as an open-source product?

title: StarSling (YC P25)
summary: Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos

extra.author: yonasb
extra.original_title: Launch HN: StarSling (YC P25) – Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos

story_text.value:
We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling (https://starsling.dev), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows.

Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost.

Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762.

I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill.

We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww.

Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry - Propose an optimization - Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change - Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant - Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence

We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time: - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x)

Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills. The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself.

We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly (https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks).

We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks.

To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start. You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes.

Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge.

We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!

title: Axonnic (YC F26)
summary: Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force

extra.author: arshpatankar
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force

story_text.value:
Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (https://axonnic.com). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots.

Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA

We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly.

The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors.

When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks.

We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies.

Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension.

Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings.

So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG.

If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks!

https://axonnic.com

So what gives?

title: anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python: v2.10.0
summary:
### Features

* **api:** add beta support for the billing_policy request parameter
* **api:** add contract_spend_limit_reached error code to messages
* **api:** add error codes for linked billing refusals
* **api:** add the user_profile_billing_not_authorized error code
* **api:** add webhook events for external key failure and recovery


### Bug Fixes

* **client:** stop reporting failed aiohttp connections as timeouts
* **types:** keep deprecated model aliases and the types nested under them working


### Chores

* **api:** rename error data models, deprecating the old names
* **docs:** clarify which AWS KMS keys a workspace can use on Claude Platform on AWS
* **docs:** clarify which credential work get, update and list accept
* **docs:** clarify which uploads a plugin pin holds back
* **docs:** note that a plugin scan's reason also covers errored scans

  `content_scan.reason` on an errored scan now says why there is no verdict. It is not a security finding, so code that treats any `reason` as a concern should also check `status`.

* **internal:** don't report moved classes as breaking changes


### Documentation

* name each SDK's own types in rename deprecations

summary: Over the past year, we’ve strengthened the default protections behind what Instagram recommends in India to reduce unwanted content and improve people’s experience on Instagram. This work has been guided by what our users told us they want from their recommendations. Today, we’re sharing an update on this work. How Recommendations Work At Instagram, we make personalized recommendations to help people discover new communities and content. Our goal is to make recommendations that are relevant and valuable to each person who sees them. For example, if you interact with restaurants and bookstores on Instagram, we may recommend content about food, recipes, books, or reading. Recommendations include content from accounts you don’t already follow, in places like Explore, Reels and Feed , so we apply guidelines specific to them. Through our Recommendations Guidelines , we work to avoid recommending content that could be low quality, objectionable or particularly sensitive. We use technology to detect content and accounts that don’t meet those guidelines and to help us avoid recommending them. As always, content that goes against our Community Standards is removed from Instagram, and content that is unlawful in a country is restricted there. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
summary: The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock . Why unneeded model calls add up The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost. title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
summary: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction. In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob , IBM , IQM , Pasqal , Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces. title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
summary: This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI. CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today. At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do. From SC06 to SC26 NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more. In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research , accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films . Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack.
